testimony.subject: Policy on issuing patents-in-fee to Indians
testimony.key_claims: Nine out of ten Indians who received patents sold their land and spent proceeds within one or two years. Nearly all bought cars after selling land. Not more than one in ten purchased teams, farm implements, or made improvements. About 600 out of 5,500 population received patents, principally in past ten years. 85% of patents covered 160 acres valued $1,000-$16,000, average $4,000. About 12-15 Indians still retain allotments. Recommended case-by-case evaluation irrespective of blood status or education. Warned against rushing process and cautioned about creating homeless paupers.

testimony.subject: Effect of patent-in-fee policy on Turtle Mountain Indians
testimony.key_claims: Government has gone too swiftly in issuance of patents-in-fee. 95% of Indians sold land as soon as they could, often at prices below real value or mortgaged it. Indians who mortgage land become discouraged, default on payments, and lose the land. Civilization should be reckoned in terms of generations. Recommended careful investigation of character and habits, with 20-40 acres held in trust for lifetime. Provided tabulation showing 1,393 patents covering 185,918.76 acres issued 1910-1921. About 3,500 Indians on reservation out of 3,400 enrolled. Allotments located in western North Dakota and eastern Montana because reservation only two townships.

testimony.subject: Condition of patent-in-fee Indians
testimony.key_claims: Indians are being released from federal supervision too rapidly. Their inability to handle business in competition with experienced white men places them at great disadvantage. Nearly all patent-in-fee Indians known to him are in worse condition than when they became independent citizens. Taxes on Indian reservations are necessarily high, exceed land income, making Indians anxious to sell. Recommended modified merit system and holding at least half of valuable allotments in trust for lifetime as home site.

testimony.subject: Certificates of competency and fee patents at Bad River Reservation
testimony.key_claims: 399 original allotments patented through certificates of competency since 1913, plus 74 heirship certificates, totaling 373 certificates. Rate increased from 4 in 1913 to 88 in 1920. Approximately 1,600 allotted Indians on reservation. 98% of those granted certificates sold their land. 80-acre allotments on former virgin forest land sold for $300-$1,500, most under $500. Trust funds also turned over averaging around $1,000. Indian is cheerful loser with no regrets. Modern educated Indians should be turned loose. Aged and dependent class and minors should be protected. About $1 million remains in trust for aged and minor Indians. About 150 Indians employed at lumber company sawmill operating 27 years on reservation.

testimony.subject: Effect of fee patents on Nez Perce Indians
testimony.key_claims: About 500 fee patents issued to Nez Perces. Prima facie competent (young educated class) first to dispose of lands and squander proceeds. Older uneducated people holding onto lands, buying other lands, even purchasing at land sales in competition with white bidders. Several full-blood Nez Perces hold mortgages on white men's farms. One full-blood woman holds $13,000 mortgage on 480 acres and $1,000 mortgage on orchard tract. One young man spent $17,000. Of 300 fee patents issued last year, estimated 200 owners sold or mortgaged land. 1,400 Indians on reservation, not 50 earning all own living. Nez Perces never received government rations. Recommends superintendents submit lists rather than wholesale patent issuance. Paradox of incompetency of the competent and competency of the incompetent. Three-fourths of Indians are thrifty, sober, law-abiding. Trust period extended ten years for most older Indians. 30,000 acres under irrigation.

testimony.subject: Effect of granting patents-in-fee to Fort Peck Indians
testimony.key_claims: Vital mistakes made in handling Indian question. Opposed to granting citizenship to Indians in bulk. Each reservation and individual case should be decided on own merit. Every family should maintain a homestead. Fort Peck Indians allotted only twelve years ago and large number now own nothing. Only way they can acquire real estate is through inheritance. Referenced Rocky Boy Indians who roamed Montana for sixty years without reservation, became degraded, state petitioned for reservation for them - illustrating that freedom alone does not lead to self-sufficiency. Referenced Fort Belknap reservation where Indians hold land in common and live in severe poverty despite splendid reservation.
